content: Patients co-infected with HIV-1 and HBV who discontinue antiretroviral therapy (ART) should undergo clinical and laboratory follow-up for several months. If necessary, initiating hepatitis B therapy may be warranted. Severe, acute exacerbations of hepatitis B have been reported in patients co-infected with HBV and HIV-1 (refer to Black Box Warnings and Dosing Considerations). It is essential to test HIV-1 patients for chronic hepatitis B virus infection before starting therapy. Drug-induced hepatitis, including acute hepatitis and cytolytic hepatitis, has been observed in clinical trials involving darunavir. Patients with preexisting liver dysfunction, such as chronic active hepatitis B or C, are at an increased risk of liver function abnormalities, including severe hepatic adverse reactions. Rare cases of severe skin reactions, such as Stevens-Johnson syndrome, toxic epidermal necrolysis, drug rash with eosinophilia and systemic symptoms (DRESS), and acute generalized exanthematous pustulosis, have been reported. These reactions may be accompanied by fever and/or elevated transaminases. Immune reconstitution syndrome has been reported in patients treated with combination antiretroviral therapy. Autoimmune disorders, including Graves’ disease, polymyositis, Guillain-Barré syndrome, and autoimmune hepatitis, have also been reported. Postmarketing cases of renal impairment, including acute renal failure, proximal renal tubulopathy (PRT), and Fanconi syndrome (characterized by renal tubular injury and severe hypophosphatemia), have been associated with the use of tenofovir prodrugs. Darunavir contains a sulfonamide moiety, so patients with a known sulfonamide allergy should be closely monitored after initiating therapy. Lactic acidosis and severe hepatomegaly with steatosis, including fatal cases, have been reported with the use of nucleoside analogs, such as emtricitabine. New-onset diabetes mellitus, worsening of preexisting diabetes mellitus, and hyperglycemia have been reported during postmarketing surveillance in HIV-infected patients receiving HIV protease inhibitor therapy. Redistribution or accumulation of body fat, including central obesity, dorsocervical fat enlargement (buffalo hump), peripheral wasting, facial wasting, breast enlargement, and a cushingoid appearance, has been observed in patients receiving ARTs. Increased bleeding, including spontaneous skin hematomas and hemarthrosis, has been reported in patients with hemophilia types A and B treated with HIV protease inhibitors. Darunavir and cobicistat are not recommended during pregnancy due to significantly lower exposures of these drugs during pregnancy. Symtuza should not be initiated in pregnant women, and an alternative regimen should be used for women who become pregnant during therapy. A pregnancy exposure registry monitors outcomes in women exposed to ARTs during pregnancy, and clinicians are encouraged to register patients by calling the Antiretroviral Pregnancy Registry (APR) at 1-800-258-4263. The CDC advises that HIV-infected mothers in the United States should not breastfeed their infants to prevent the risk of postnatal HIV-1 transmission. Darunavir is a protease inhibitor that selectively inhibits the cleavage of Gag-Pol polyprotein precursors, thereby preventing the formation of mature virus particles. Cobicistat is a CYP3A4 inhibitor and a pharmacokinetic enhancer that increases the systemic exposure of CYP3A substrates, such as darunavir, by reducing their metabolism. Emtricitabine is a nucleoside reverse transcriptase inhibitor (NRTI) that, after phosphorylation, interferes with HIV viral DNA polymerase and inhibits viral replication. Tenofovir alafenamide (AF) is an NRTI prodrug of tenofovir that demonstrates high antiviral efficacy at a lower dose compared to tenofovir disoproxil fumarate (DF), with improved renal and bone safety profiles. It inhibits HIV-1 reverse transcriptase by competing with the natural substrate deoxyadenosine 5′-triphosphate and causes DNA chain termination after incorporation into DNA. The bioavailability of the components is not affected when administered orally as a split tablet compared to a whole tablet. Darunavir is metabolized by CYP3A, while cobicistat is metabolized primarily by CYP3A and to a lesser extent by CYP2D6. Emtricitabine is not significantly metabolized and is eliminated primarily through glomerular filtration and active tubular secretion. Tenofovir AF is hydrolyzed within cells to form tenofovir by cathepsin A and is minimally metabolized by CYP3A in the liver. The medication should be taken with food. If unable to swallow the whole tablet, it can be split into two pieces using a tablet cutter, and the entire dose should be consumed immediately after splitting. Store the medication at 20–25°C (68–77°F), with excursions permitted to 15–30°C (59–86°F). Keep the container tightly closed with a desiccant inside to protect from moisture. Dispense only in the original container. Adding plans allows for comparison of formulary status with other drugs in the same class.
